title: Non-Hermitian Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm
abstract: Non-Hermitian systems offer new opportunities for quantum optimization and computation. Here, we show that non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic algorithms require not only a real, gapped spectrum, but also a stable pseudospectrum. We propose a novel framework by mapping non-unitary quantum circuits to local Hamiltonian paths, thereby preserving their optimization advantages and shallow depth. While a direct non-Hermitian extension of the Feynman-Kitaev construction suffers severe pseudospectral instability, our history-decoupled construction yields both a controlled pseudospectrum and a real, gapped spectrum. Using the CK benchmark family of maximum independent set problems, we demonstrate polynomial-evolution-time non-Hermitian adiabatic computation that remains robust against perturbations. We further discuss a feasible optical implementation using coupled waveguides with an auxiliary lossy channel. Our work establishes pseudospectral stability, alongside real, gapped spectra, as key principles and a practical route for non-Hermitian quantum adiabatic computation.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, stable framework for Non-Hermitian Quantum Adiabatic Algorithms. By proposing a history-decoupled mapping, it overcomes critical spectral instabilities found in previous non-Hermitian approaches. This work establishes pseudospectral stability as a key requirement, offering a practical route for quantum computation suitable for current noisy hardware.
main_problem: Developing a robust non-Hermitian Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm (QAA) that overcomes spectral instabilities inherent in standard adiabatic quantum computation methods.
main_result: The authors propose a history-decoupled construction (HD QAA) which successfully maintains both pseudospectral stability and a real, gapped spectrum for non-Hermitian evolution.
method: They map non-unitary quantum circuits to local Hamiltonian paths using a novel 'history-decoupled' mapping, avoiding the severe instabilities of direct extensions like the Feynman-Kitaev construction.
model_or_system: The work focuses on abstract non-Hermitian Hamiltonians governing adiabatic evolution for optimization problems, benchmarked against Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problems. The underlying physics involves open quantum systems with gain/loss mechanisms.
key_observables: Real and gapped spectrum ($\Delta(s)$), stable pseudospectrum ($\Lambda_\epsilon(H)$), and polynomial evolution time.
important_parameters: The degree of spectral instability quantified by the condition number $\kappa(S)$, and the circuit depth $L$ (which dictates complexity).
main_assumptions: A real, gapped spectrum alone is insufficient; pseudospectral stability is a necessary key principle for practical non-Hermitian QAA.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates mapping QC gates to continuous Hamiltonian paths. Table I compares three constructions (HM QAA, FK QAA, HD QAA) based on adiabatic time and pseudospectrum stability.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical necessity of pseudospectral stability for non-Hermitian QAA, contrasts it with unstable methods like FK construction, proposes the stable HD mapping, and validates its polynomial scaling using MIS benchmarks.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant as it provides a concrete, theoretically sound pathway to implementing quantum algorithms on hardware that naturally supports dissipation (like Rydberg arrays), bypassing the exponential overheads associated with purely unitary models.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. A schematic illustration of the mapping from QC to QAA, where the gate sequence of the QC (top left) is con- verted to a continuous Hamiltonian path H(s) (right) from Hinit to Hfinal (lower left). The spectrum remains gapped ∆(s) = E1(s) −E0(s), thereby protecting the adiabatic evo- lution of the ground state, which, upon reaching Hfinal, yields the target solution.

FIG. 2. (a) A gap with an isolated (merged) pseudospectrum is stable (unstable) under perturbations. (b) The non-Hermitian Hatano-Nelson model exhibits a highly unstable pseudospectrum, thus the non-Hermitian skin effect and sensitivity to pertur- bations such as boundary conditions. (c) The FK QAA’s effective model resembles a non-reciprocal Hatano-Nelson chain, in which the non-normality of the similarity transformation accumulates, leading to an unstable pseudospectrum. (d) In com- parison, the HD QAA converts non-unitary gates Vl and V −1 l and establishes non-reciprocal coupling locally, thereby ensuring overall pseudospectral stability and, thus, adiabaticity under perturbations.

FIG. 3. A schematic illustration of the CK graph (Gm, m = 3) and its modifications (G′ m, m = 3) of the MIS problem. Solid black circles represent vertices, and lines represent edges. In the CK graph G3, the left (isolated dots) and right (triangles) sections are fully connected (both solid and dashed lines). Its MIS consists of the three vertices on the left, while the trian- gles on the right generate competing local minima. A CK-like graph G′ 3 is obtained by randomly removing connections (or- ange dashed lines) between the G3’s two sides.

FIG. 4. A schematic illustration of the non-unitary QC for solving the MIS problem: given an initial state |ψ0⟩with equal-weight superposition |+⟩⊗n, the output is obtained af- ter repeated r rounds of operations. Within each round (dashed box), vertex-amplification gates Ai(p) and two-qubit edge-constraint gates Bjk(q) are applied according to the ver- tices and edges of the MIS graph.

FIG. 5. The success probability P (0) MIS of the three QAAs exhibits qualitatively different scalings versus the problem size n. The HM QAA (green, right log axis) suffers an exponential decrease, whereas the non-Hermitian QAAs’ P (0) MIS (left linear axis) decrease much more slowly. Note the difference in the vertical axis. Still, the HD QAA (orange) leads with a success probability P (0) MIS ∼1 versus the polynomial scaling of the FK QAA (blue). Here, the solid lines indicate results on the CK graphs Gm, while the dashed lines and shaded regions denote the medians and the ranges across 200 CK-like graphs G′ m.
